# Dark Web Trends 2026: 5 Threats Reshaping the Cyber Underground


Cyble breaks down how dark web ecosystems are evolving in 2026 with ransomware, initial access brokers, AI-driven attacks, and underground threat activity.


July 8, 2026 · 9 min read


**Dark Web Trends 2026 at a glance:** Government data published in 2026 points to five shifts in the dark web threat landscape: a ransomware market dominated by a few big brands but constantly churning underneath, an industrialized infostealer and initial access pipeline, phishing and stolen credentials as the main way in, nation-state campaigns that borrow criminal infrastructure, and AI built into criminal services. Together they show the dark web now works as cybercrime’s operational hub, not just a place to dump stolen data.


## **Key Takeaways**


- The FBI received 3,611 ransomware complaints in 2025, up from 3,156 in 2024, and identified 63 new ransomware variants.
- Europol observed more than 120 active ransomware brands in 2025, with affiliates working across several brands at once.
- Operation Endgame (June 2026) took down 326 servers and recovered about 27 million stolen credentials from infostealer infrastructure.
- Phishing remains the top way in: 43% of UK businesses reported a breach or attack in 2025/26, and 38% were hit by phishing.
- Nation states now drive most of the UK’s nationally significant incidents, and US agencies linked Iranian attacks on industrial controls to the 2026 hostilities.
- The FBI began tracking AI-enabled crime in 2025, logging $893 million in related losses.


The dark web is no longer just a marketplace for stolen credentials; it has grown far beyond that point and now affects nearly every phase of the cyberattack lifecycle. Markets that once traded only compromised accounts now also sell ransomware services, initial network access, exploit kits, phishing infrastructure, and even AI-powered attack tools.


What used to be a place for selling stolen data has become the operational backbone of modern cybercrime.


The first half of 2026 alone is indicative of the trends we may continue to observe. The dark web has evolved into a highly organized ecosystem that facilitates cybercrime, underpins[ransomware](https://cyble.com/knowledge-hub/what-is-ransomware/) supply chains, fuels geopolitical campaigns, and accelerates identity-based attacks.


Instead of serving as the endpoint for stolen data, it now functions as an operational hub where access, intelligence, and malicious services are traded before attacks even begin.


The pace of activity reflects this shift:[March 2026](https://cyble.com/blog/monthly-threat-landscape-march-2026/) alone recorded 702 ransomware attacks and 54 major publicly reported data breaches and leaks worldwide.


Enterprise security teams must monitor such activities using continuous threat intel and underground monitoring. The current ecosystem is no longer optional as an intel exercise but an essential capability for spotting threats before they materialize.


The dark web trends observed during the first half of 2026 reveal how underground ecosystems are reshaping the[cyber threat landscape](https://cyble.com/blog/2026-threat-intelligence-trends/) .


## 1. Ransomware: Dominant Brands, Constant Churn


Ransomware remains one of the most disruptive threats, and government data shows a market that is concentrated at the top but unstable underneath. The FBI received 3,611 ransomware complaints in 2025, up from 3,156 in 2024 and 2,825 in 2023. The top ten variants accounted for 56% of reported incidents, led by Akira, Qilin, INC Ransom/Lynx/Sinobi, BianLian and Play.


Yet the churn is constant. The FBI identified 63 new ransomware variants in 2025, and Europol observed more than 120 active ransomware brands over the same year. Europol describes the ecosystem as fragmented, competitive and adaptable, with new brands appearing after law enforcement disruptions and affiliates and administrators working across multiple brands at once.


The damage is broad. Every one of the 16 US critical infrastructure sectors reported ransomware attacks to the FBI in 2025, with healthcare, manufacturing, financial services, government and IT among the most targeted. Reported ransomware losses more than doubled to about $32.3 million, and the FBI notes this excludes downtime, lost business and remediation costs.


Data theft is now standard in these attacks. Dark web leak sites are where stolen information is published or auctioned when victims refuse to pay, so monitoring them gives early warning of exposure, targeting and upcoming[campaigns](https://cyble.com/blog/new-ransomware-groups-on-the-rise/) .


## 2. Initial Access Brokers Fuel the Underground Economy


Many[cyberattacks](https://cyble.com/knowledge-hub/what-is-a-cyber-attack/) now start long before ransomware is deployed. Initial access brokers compromise networks and sell that access, while infostealer malware harvests the passwords, cookies and session tokens that feed underground markets.


Law enforcement is now going after this layer directly. In June 2026, the latest phase of Operation Endgame dismantled the infrastructure behind three malware families central to initial access: SocGholish, Amadey and StealC. Authorities took down 326 servers and 142 domains, recovered about 27 million stolen credentials from more than 385,000 infected systems, and froze more than €41 million (about $47 million) in criminal cryptocurrency. Agencies from Germany, the Netherlands, Denmark, the UK, the US and Canada took part, supported by Europol and Eurojust.


The market recovers fast, though. Europol reports that criminal marketplaces stay highly resilient: new platforms emerge quickly, and forums help users and vendors migrate after a takedown.


Ransomware groups and espionage operators no longer need to breach organisations themselves; they can buy verified entry points. Because access is sold soon after a compromise, defenders have little time to act. Dark web intelligence helps here by showing not just stolen data but signs that access to a network is already being traded.


Access is typically sold soon after a compromise, so defenders have less time to detect exposed credentials or compromised infrastructure. ## 3. Identity Becomes the Primary Attack Surface


Credential-based attacks have made the traditional perimeter far less relevant. Credential theft, session hijacking, MFA bypass and abuse of third-party access all rely on one thing: valid credentials. Logging in with legitimate credentials draws far less suspicion than exploiting a vulnerability.


Government data confirms that phishing and stolen credentials remain the main way in. The UK government’s Cyber Security Breaches Survey 2025/26, published in April 2026, found that 43% of businesses (about 612,000) reported a breach or attack in the past year. Phishing was the most common, hitting 38% of businesses.


In the US, data breaches were the top cyber threat reported to the FBI in 2025 at 39%, followed by ransomware at 36% and SIM swapping at 10%. SIM swapping matters here because it is a common way to bypass SMS-based multi-factor authentication.


The scale of the credential supply is visible in law enforcement seizures. The 27 million stolen credentials recovered in Operation Endgame show how directly infostealers feed the trade in usernames, passwords, tokens and corporate accounts. Monitoring for exposed credentials lets organisations respond before those identities are used against them.

## 4. Geopolitics Drives Cyber Campaigns


The link between global conflict and cyber activity became hard to miss in 2026. State-sponsored groups, hacktivists and financially motivated criminals often operate side by side during periods of tension, and many sophisticated actors are investing in long-term access to critical infrastructure.


In April 2026, the FBI, CISA, NSA, EPA, Department of Energy and US Cyber Command issued joint advisory AA26-097A. It warned that Iranian-affiliated actors were exploiting internet-exposed programmable logic controllers (PLCs) across US critical infrastructure, and that this targeting had escalated, likely in response to hostilities between Iran, the United States and Israel. A July 2026 update reported that the actors modified and deleted PLC project logic and manipulated data on HMI and SCADA displays.


The UK sees the same shift. At CYBERUK 2026, the head of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said ransomware is still the most common threat for most organisations, but that most of the nationally significant incidents the NCSC handles now come directly or indirectly from nation states. New Zealand’s NCSC reported that 86 of the 369 incidents of potential national significance in the year to June 2026 had suspected links to state-sponsored actors.


Europol adds that hybrid threat actors increasingly use criminal networks as proxies for DDoS, ransomware and data theft. This blending of political and criminal goals makes attribution harder and raises the value of watching underground discussions that may signal a campaign before it reaches production systems.

## 5. AI Accelerates Attackers and Defenders


AI has moved from experiment to everyday use on both sides. Attackers use it to automate reconnaissance, speed up exploitation and scale phishing with greater precision.


Government agencies now measure and forecast this directly. The FBI added AI-enabled crime as a reporting category in 2025 and logged $893 million in related losses. Europol reports that ransomware-as-a-service groups are adding AI tools to their offerings to attract affiliates, and that generative AI is making scams more convincing and personalised. New Zealand’s NCSC, in its Cyber Threat Report 2026, expects the most capable AI tools to speed up zero-day discovery, automate reconnaissance and brute-force attacks, and make phishing and deepfakes more convincing.


The dark web has become a marketplace for AI-enabled attack tools alongside traditional malware, which lowers the skill barrier and speeds up operations. Defenders are responding in kind, using automated analysis to process large volumes of dark web data, spot indicators of compromise and prioritise threats in near real time.


The question is no longer whether your organisation appears on the dark web. It is whether you find out before your attackers act.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Dark Web Trends 2026


1.


##### **What is the biggest dark web trend in 2026?**


The clearest trend is ransomware consolidation: five operators — Qilin, Akira, The Gentlemen, DragonForce, and INC Ransom — accounted for more than 56% of all ransomware activity recorded in March 2026, while data-leak extortion has become a standard part of nearly every campaign.


2.


##### **Why are initial access brokers important in 2026?**


Initial access brokers sell verified, ready-made entry points into corporate networks, letting ransomware and espionage actors skip the breach step entirely. Researchers tracked 80 separate access listings in March 2026 alone, with government, professional services, manufacturing, and retail as the most targeted sectors.


3.


##### **How is AI changing dark web activity in 2026?**


AI is lowering the skill barrier for attackers, who now use it to automate reconnaissance and scale phishing with greater precision, while the same tools are helping defenders process dark web data and flag indicators of compromise faster.


4.


##### **How can organizations monitor dark web threats in 2026?**


Effective monitoring combines continuous dark web and underground-forum tracking with credential-exposure and initial-access-broker monitoring.[Cyble’s Dark Web Monitoring](https://cyble.com/solutions/dark-web-monitoring/) solution tracks all three across 50+ countries.


## Conclusion


The first half of 2026 stresses that the dark web is no longer where stolen information appears after an incident. It has evolved into a live intelligence environment where attacks are planned, infrastructure is traded, identities are monetized, and emerging tactics become visible before they reach production networks.


Organizations that incorporate dark web intelligence into broader security operations gain more than visibility into compromised data; they gain early warning of evolving threats.


As ransomware groups become more coordinated, identity attacks continue to rise, and AI reshapes offensive capabilities, proactive monitoring will play an important role in reducing cyber risk during the remainder of 2026.
